passage_text: Researchers studied the effects of a novel antioxidant compound, Antiox-1, on cultured human fibroblasts exposed to oxidative stress. Fibroblasts were divided into four groups: a control group receiving no compound, a group treated with Antiox-1 at 10 µM (Treatment A), a group treated with Antiox-1 at 50 µM (Treatment B), and a group treated with a known antioxidant, N-acetylcysteine (NAC) at 20 µM (Treatment C). After 24 hours of exposure to 200 µM hydrogen peroxide, researchers measured cell viability, apoptosis rate, reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, and mitochondrial membrane potential. Results indicated that Antiox-1 at 50 µM produced the highest cell viability and lowest apoptosis rate, while NAC showed intermediate effects. ROS levels were markedly reduced in both Antiox-1 treatments compared to control, with the 50 µM dose achieving the greatest reduction. Mitochondrial membrane potential was preserved in the Antiox-1 50 µM group, suggesting a protective effect on mitochondrial function. These findings suggest that Antiox-1, particularly at higher concentrations, may offer superior protection against oxidative damage in fibroblasts, warranting further investigation in vivo.
stem: Which treatment group exhibited the highest cell viability after exposure to oxidative stress?
explanation: The table shows that the 50 µM Antiox-1 group (Treatment B) achieved 84 % viability, the highest among all groups.
trap: A common mistake is to select the NAC group (D) because it is a known antioxidant, but its viability (78 %) is lower than that of the 50 µM Antiox-1 group.

stem: Which comparison isolates the effect of Antiox-1 concentration, with the compound itself held constant?
explanation: Correct: C) Treatments A and B both use Antiox-1 and differ only in concentration (10 vs. 50 µM). Why the others are wrong: A) Control vs. Treatment A compares the presence versus absence of the compound. B) Control vs. Treatment C tests NAC against no treatment and says nothing about Antiox-1. D) Treatment B vs. Treatment C differs in both compound and concentration, so the two cannot be separated.
trap: Choosing the comparison with the untreated control (option A), which shows only that the compound has an effect, not how the effect changes with concentration.

trap: Choosing 40% (option A), which is the remaining ROS fraction (60/150) rather than the reduction (90/150 = 60%).

stem: Which of the following statements incorrectly interprets the data?

options.A: Antiox-1 at 50 µM provides the greatest protection against oxidative stress.
options.B: The 10 µM dose of Antiox-1 is less effective than NAC.
options.C: ROS levels are lowest in the control group.
options.D: Mitochondrial membrane potential is highest in Treatment B.

explanation: The table shows ROS levels are 150 µM in control, 110 µM in Treatment A, 60 µM in Treatment B, and 90 µM in Treatment C. Thus, ROS is lowest in Treatment B, not the control.
trap: Accepting 'ROS lowest in control' because untreated cells serve as the baseline; under peroxide stress the control actually had the highest ROS (150 µM).

stem: Which limitation most restricts applying these findings to patients?

options.A: The compound was tested only in cultured fibroblasts exposed to hydrogen peroxide, not in a whole-organism disease model.
options.B: The control group received no compound.
options.C: NAC was included as a comparator.
options.D: Four different outcome measures were recorded.

explanation: Correct: A) Cultured fibroblasts under hydrogen peroxide stress do not reproduce a whole-organism disease, which is why the passage calls for in vivo work. Why the others are wrong: B) An untreated control is a needed design element, not a limitation. C) A known antioxidant comparator strengthens the design. D) Measuring several outcomes does not limit applicability to patients.
trap: Picking a specific disease application such as myocardial infarction because cell protection sounds clinically relevant; the data come only from cultured fibroblasts.
